ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A light rope of length $l$ has one end fixed at point $O$ and the other end attached to a small ball of mass $m$. The ball is thrown horizontally to the right from point $A$, which is at the same height as point $O$, with a certain initial velocity. After some time, the rope becomes taut, and thereafter, the ball swings in a vertical plane with $O$ as the center. It is known that the distance $OA$ is $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}l$, and the angle between the rope and the vertical direction when the rope just becomes taut is $60^\circ$. The gravitational acceleration is $g$, and air resistance is negligible.

1. The velocity of the small ball when it is thrown and the velocity at the instant when the rope becomes taut; do not add any other content.
2. When the small ball swings to the lowest point, the magnitude of the tension force exerted by the string on the ball.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure the fixed point O is at a relatively high position, point A is to the left of O and at the same height as O, and the small ball is thrown horizontally to the right from A; the string is initially slack, and afterward is pulled taut at a certain point to the lower right of O. In the figure a vertical dashed line is drawn downward from O, and when the string is pulled taut it is along the oblique-line direction from O to the small ball at the lower right, and the angle between this oblique line and the vertically downward direction is marked as 60°. Then reason: According to the specified method, take O as the origin, the x-axis to the right as positive, and the y-axis upward as positive. From the image and the problem statement, A is at the same height as O and to the left of O, OA=√3l/2, so the coordinates of A are (-√3l/2,0). When the string has just been pulled taut, the small ball is at point B, OB=l, and OB makes an angle of 60° with the vertically downward direction, so the coordinates of B are (l sin60°,-l cos60°)=(√3l/2,-l/2). The displacement from A to B is Δx=√3l, Δy=-l/2. The small ball is thrown horizontally from A, therefore in the vertical direction it satisfies -l/2=-(1/2)gt^2, giving t=√(l/g). In the horizontal direction Δx=v0t, so v0=√3l/√(l/g)=√(3gl). Just before the string is pulled taut, the velocity components are vx=v0=√(3gl), vy=-gt=-√(gl), so the velocity vector is √(gl)(√3,-1). And the unit vector in the OB direction is (sin60°,-cos60°)=(√3/2,-1/2), so it can be seen that at this time the velocity is completely along the radial direction of OB, and the tangential component is 0. The impulse from the string suddenly being pulled taut eliminates the radial velocity, so the velocity just after the string is pulled taut is 0. Afterward the small ball starts from rest at point B and swings around O. The vertical drop height from point B to the lowest point is l-lcos60°=l/2. By conservation of mechanical energy, the square of the velocity at the lowest point is v^2=2g(l/2)=gl. At the lowest point, in the radial direction there is T-mg=mv^2/l=mgl/l=mg, so T=2mg.
